images.caption: 'STEAM' museum, Kemble Drive, Swindon The museum celebrates the years between 1843 and 1986 when Swindon was home to the Great Western Railway manufacturing centre where locomotives, carriages and wagons were built and repaired. It is housed in what used to be 'R' shop. A feature of the museum is the use of tableaux to illustrate a facet of life in the works. In this one a tardy worker is being disciplined by the loss of half a day's pay.

images.caption: Model of GWR Dean "Lord of the Isles" Class 4-2-2 No.3048 "Majestic" built 1895 and withdrawn 1913. The first 8 locos of the class were built as "Convertible" "Achilles" Class 2-2-2's, that is, they were built as Broad Gauge locos in 1891 with the facility to be converted to Standard Gauge, which they were in 1892 (as "Lord of the Isles" Class 4-2-2's). At "Steam", Swindon 7/07.
images.alt: Model of GWR Dean "Lord of the Isles" Class 4-2-2 No.3048 "Majestic" built 1895 and withdrawn 1913. The first 8 locos of the class were built as "Convertible" "Achilles" Class 2-2-2's, that is, they were built as Broad Gauge locos in 1891 with the facility to be converted to Standard Gauge, which they were in 1892 (as "Lord of the Isles" Class 4-2-2's). At "Steam", Swindon 7/07.

images.caption: Model of G.J. Churchward's magnicantly flawed 4-6-2 - the first British Pacific - No.111 "The Great Bear" at the Swindon Steam Museum 7/07. The only design Churchward produced that was a failure but even then it could have formed the basis of a successful design if there had been a need for such a powerful engine but as it was the superb "Star" 4-6-0's could handle anything hung behind them with ease and efficiency.
images.alt: Model of G.J. Churchward's magnicantly flawed 4-6-2 - the first British Pacific - No.111 "The Great Bear" at the Swindon Steam Museum 7/07. The only design Churchward produced that was a failure but even then it could have formed the basis of a successful design if there had been a need for such a powerful engine but as it was the superb "Star" 4-6-0's could handle anything hung behind them with ease and efficiency.

images.caption: Model of Crampton 4-2-0 165 "George K. Gale", which may have been made by Crampton himself whilst at the G.W.R. Swindon Works working for Sir Daniel Gooch. On display at the same works - but now the Steam museum, 7/09. It is not clear whether the model represents a locomotive that was built or was a proposal or was merely an exercise to demonstrate the Crampton design. I can find no record of such a locomotive being built or even of a man named George K. Gale and it is not a Great Wetsern engine. It looks a little like the "London" built at Crewe in 1846 for the Southern Division of the LNWR and the livery of the model seems to be LNWR (SD) Vermillion. However, the "London" had many detail differences from George K. Gale (e.g. the steam pipes) and would have been in LNWR (SD) Green as the Vermillion was not introduced until some time later. A mystery.
